angle: Material porosity, water absorption standards (ASTM C373 / ISO 10545-3 / ASTM C242), ceramic moisture uptake and steam release in unglazed clay bakers, and moisture retention vs. evaporation behavior across slow-cook vessels over 2-, 4-, and 8-hour intervals.

findings.claim: Unglazed terracotta / low-fired earthenware open (apparent) porosity and water absorption
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Values vary strongly with peak firing temperature (typically 850-1050 C) and carbonate/flux content; raising firing from ~900 C to >1000 C closes open pores and can drop water absorption from ~8.7% to ~3.8% in fluxed red clays, whereas coarse low-fired wares exceed 20%.
sources: ASTM C373 / ISO 10545-3 & ISO 13006 (Group BIII >10% water absorption)
MDPI Materials / Applied Sciences / Ceramics studies on fired red clay and terracotta bodies
Construction and Building Materials / Ceramics International terracotta durability literature
findings.unit: % (mass % for water absorption; volume % for apparent open porosity)
findings.value_or_range: Water absorption: 8-25% (full earthenware span ~4% to >25%; architectural/traditional terracotta commonly 8-15%). Apparent open porosity: 15-35% (denser cookware formulations ~12-25%).

findings.claim: Unglazed Zisha (Yixing purple clay) open/apparent porosity and water absorption
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Dicaoqing-Zisha fired at 1180 C shows dual-scale pores (~0.2 um and <10 nm), making it impermeable to bulk liquid water yet gas-permeable. Reported ~10.79%/11% porosity and ~2.1% water absorption come from Sun et al. (2024) / cited Zisha testing, while other ceramic sources report 3-5% water absorption for hand-crafted Zisha (~1% for high-fired machine ware) and 3-12% open porosity; exact values vary by ore (Zini, Dicaoqing, Benshanzhu) and firing temp (1100-1200 C).
sources: Yang et al. (2021), Ceramics International 47(8):10650-10657 (DOI: 10.1016/j.ceramint.2020.12.178)
Sun et al. (2024), Environment-Behaviour Proceedings Journal 9(SI23)
Terebess / Yixing ceramic engineering summaries
findings.value_or_range: Water absorption: ~2.1% to 6.0% (typical hand-built range 3-5%; high-fired down to ~1%; coarse/low-fired variants up to ~10.8%). Apparent porosity: ~4-12% (measured ~10.8-11% in cited Dicaoqing/Zisha samples).

findings.claim: La Chamba burnished micaceous clay open porosity and water absorption
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: EVIDENCE GAP: Neither Colombia's SIC Denomination of Origin dossier nor Miller et al. (2020) Scientific Reports publishes ASTM C373 water absorption (%) or open porosity (%) specifically measured on La Chamba vessels. SIC documents that La Chamba uses a three-clay blend (lisa, arenosa, and a red-clay engobe explicitly applied to reduce porosity and waterproof walls), stone-burnishing, 750-800 C firing, and organic reduction smoking to seal surface pores. Unseasoned earthenware of this class is widely assumed at ~10-15% water absorption (unverified estimate), while a peer-reviewed SciELO Brasil MIP study of low-fired micaceous archaeological potsherds measured 21-26% apparent porosity (void ratio 0.28-0.36).
sources: Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (SIC), Colombia - Ceramica Negra de La Chamba Denomination of Origin
Miller et al. (2020), Scientific Reports (La Chamba 1-year cooking lipid absorption experiment)
SciELO Brasil (MIP porosity study of megalithic micaceous potsherds)
findings.value_or_range: No direct La Chamba lab measurement found (LOW CONFIDENCE). Firing temp: 750-800 C (SIC). Analog low-fired micaceous potsherds (MIP): 21-26% porosity.

findings.claim: Vitrified glazed stoneware open porosity and water absorption
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Distinguish glaze from body: an intact vitrified glaze forms an impermeable glass surface (~0% open porosity), while the underlying stoneware body spans impervious/porcelain stoneware (<=0.5% WA) to vitreous stoneware (0.5-3.0% WA) and semivitreous stoneware (3.0-7.0% WA per ASTM C242/C373 & ANSI A137.1; 3-6% Group BIIa per ISO 13006). Boil tests (ASTM C373 / ISO 10545-3) can slightly under-measure micro-open porosity compared to gas pycnometry.
sources: ASTM C242 (vitreous/semivitreous stoneware definitions) & ASTM C373 / ANSI A137.1
ISO 13006 & ISO 10545-3 (Groups BIa and BIb)
MDPI Materials / Ceramics / Applied Sciences studies on porcelain stoneware
findings.value_or_range: Porcelain/impervious vitrified stoneware: <=0.5% water absorption (typically 0.05-0.5%), <0.5-2.0% apparent porosity (often <0.6%). Vitreous stoneware: 0.5-3.0% water absorption. Semivitreous stoneware: 3.0-7.0% water absorption.

findings.claim: Water absorbed and released by a soaked Romertopf clay baker into the cooking chamber
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: EVIDENCE GAP: Official Romertopf manuals (roemertopf.de) prescribe a 10-20 min (typically 15 min) cold-water soak before placing into a cold oven, but neither Romertopf, Stiftung Warentest, nor major test kitchens (Cook's Illustrated, Serious Eats) publish gravimetric measurements (g, ml, or %) of water absorbed or the split vented inward to food vs. outward into the oven. Unverified culinary/mass-balance estimates based on 10-15% terracotta absorption on a 3.5-4.5 kg dry baker suggest ~350-675 ml at saturation (~180-350 ml for a 15-min soak on 3-4 qt models), tagged LOW CONFIDENCE.
sources: Romertopf official care and usage instructions (roemertopf.de / manuals.plus)
Stiftung Warentest search confirmation (no dedicated Romertopf water-absorption test published)
ASTM C373 / terracotta porosity literature (for theoretical upper-bound context only)
findings.unit: minutes soak; ml or g water (theoretical/unverified)
findings.value_or_range: Prescribed soak: 10-20 min (HIGH confidence). Exact water absorbed & chamber release fraction: unmeasured in authoritative sources (~180-675 ml theoretical/informal range, LOW CONFIDENCE).

findings.claim: Moisture and evaporation loss over 2-, 4-, and 8-hour slow cooks: unglazed clay vs. glazed stoneware vs. metal Dutch ovens/multi-cookers
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: EVIDENCE GAP: No peer-reviewed study or test kitchen publishes a controlled 2h/4h/8h side-by-side gravimetric moisture-loss table across all three vessel types on an identical recipe. Verified comparative mechanics: (1) Glazed stoneware electric slow cookers form a near-closed condensation loop with minimal evaporation over 4-8h; meat/vegetable purge (70-80% water) increases free liquid, requiring 30-50% less added liquid than Dutch ovens (minimum ~0.5-1 cup). Lifting the lid vents steam and adds 20-30 min cooking time per peek. (2) Heavy Dutch ovens in 250-325 F ovens allow gradual vapor escape and sauce reduction over 2-4h; cracking the lid ajar drops braising liquid equilibrium from ~210 F (sealed) to ~190 F via evaporative cooling; loose lids/extended cooks risk dry-out by 4-8h (single non-peer-reviewed cookware comparison cites ~20-25% loss over 2.5-3.5h). (3) Multi-cookers have near-zero evaporation under pressure (>=1 cup minimum liquid required), while slow-cook mode heats from the bottom rather than wrap-around walls, raising scorching risk. (4) Soaked unglazed clay is suited to 1-3h oven cooks rather than unmonitored 8h holds once wall water depletes.
sources: Colorado State, NC State, Kansas State, Michigan State, and Missouri University Extension slow-cooker publications
J. Kenji Lopez-Alt (Serious Eats / The Food Lab) braising lid-ajar temperature & evaporation tests
America's Test Kitchen / Cook's Illustrated slow cooker vs. Dutch oven recipe conversion rules
findings.value_or_range: Slow cooker added-liquid reduction vs. Dutch oven: 30-50% less (min 0.5-1 cup). Sealed vs. ajar Dutch oven liquid temp at 250 F: ~210 F vs. ~190 F. Slow-cooker lid-lift penalty: 20-30 min/peek. Direct 2/4/8h % loss table across vessels: unmeasured gap (LOW CONFIDENCE).

findings.claim: Conditions under which cooks must top up cooking liquid
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Top-ups depend on vessel seal, heat source geometry, and thermal-shock tolerance. Cold liquid must never be poured into hot unglazed clay (Romertopf, La Chamba) because rapid steam expansion and thermal shock can crack the pot.
sources: Romertopf official usage manuals (thermal shock warning)
America's Test Kitchen / Cook's Illustrated & Serious Eats braising guides
University Extension slow-cooker and multi-cooker guidelines
findings.value_or_range: Must top up / ensure minimum liquid when: (1) Dutch oven braising >3-4h (especially 4-8h) at >=300-325 F or with lid ajar/loose-fitting (add 0.5-1 cup hot liquid if level drops toward scorching); (2) Metal multi-cookers in pressure mode (<1 cup initial liquid fails to pressurize) or bottom-heated slow-cook mode with low-moisture solids; (3) Do NOT routinely top up glazed stoneware slow cookers (<10% loss; wait until meats/veg purge water), and NEVER add cold liquid to hot unglazed clay (Romertopf/La Chamba).

myths_checked: Myth: Slow cookers need just as much added broth as Dutch ovens because they cook for 8 hours. Checked: False. University Extensions and America's Test Kitchen / Serious Eats show slow cookers trap steam in a condensation loop with minimal evaporation, so meats/vegetables purge water and dilute sauces unless added liquid is cut by 30-50%.

Myth: A tight-lidded Dutch oven keeps braising liquid gentler and cooler than a cracked lid. Checked: False (or counterintuitive). Serious Eats testing shows a tightly sealed Dutch oven at 250 F allows liquid to reach ~210 F (near boiling), whereas cracking the lid ajar introduces evaporative cooling that lowers liquid temperature to ~190 F while concentrating sauce.

Myth: Yixing Zisha clay behaves like porous terracotta or leaks water. Checked: False. Yang et al. (2021, Ceramics International) and Sun et al. (2024) show Zisha fired at ~1150-1180 C has ~2-5% water absorption and ~4-11% apparent porosity in a dual-pore structure (~0.2 um and <10 nm) that is impermeable to bulk liquid water while remaining gas-permeable.

Myth: Official Romertopf or test-kitchen documentation proves exact milliliter water-release curves for clay bakers. Checked: False. Romertopf manuals prescribe a 10-20 min soak and cold-oven start, and no Stiftung Warentest, Cook's Illustrated, or peer-reviewed dataset reports exact grams absorbed or fraction vented inward vs. outward.

Myth: La Chamba pottery is glazed or completely non-porous. Checked: False. Colombian SIC Denomination of Origin records confirm it is unglazed earthenware fired at 750-800 C; porosity is reduced (not eliminated) using a red-clay engobe, stone-burnishing, and organic reduction smoking, and Miller et al. (2020, Scientific Reports) proved its walls absorb cooking lipids over time.
